stories.topic: From a Shoegaze Playlist Back to a Lost 90s Love
stories.summary: While Amit was listening heavily to Yo La Tengo, Spotify kept recommending 'shoegaze' playlists, a word he didn't know. His habit is to let random playlists run and explore whatever grabs him, and a band called Galaxie 500 hooked him. That set off a flashback. In early-to-mid-90s India, where Deep Purple and Michael Jackson were everywhere and alternative rock was hard to find, one of his favourite bands was Luna, fronted by Dean Wareham. He had a vague idea Wareham had an earlier band but could never get hold of it. That band was Galaxie 500. He then explains the genre's name: feedback-heavy, effects-laden guitars, indistinct vocals, and performers who stood still on stage staring at the pedals at their feet.
stories.insight: Amit was adventurous with books and films but stuck in a comfort zone with music. Letting an algorithm's randomness act as a discovery engine broke that habit, and it also closed a loop in his own past that scarcity had left open for 30 years.
stories.quote: With books, movies, I'm checking out new stuff. With music I was in a comfort zone

stories.topic: What Are the Two Most Recent Songs You Know?
stories.summary: Ajay and a friend worked through a question: what are the two most recent songs you know and love? His instinctive answer was November Rain, from 1992. On careful thought he found exactly two newer ones: Harry Styles' 'Sign of the Times' (2017) and Lady Gaga's 'Shallow' (2018), the second of which he struggled to name. He credits YouTube Music for bringing new music into his life.
stories.insight: It is a quick, funny self-audit of how musical taste freezes at a certain age. For both hosts, recommendation algorithms are what pry open the time capsule.
stories.quote: I actually thought carefully about it and I discovered I know one song, I know and love one song from 2017 and one song from 2018.

stories.summary: Retelling a story from Steven Pinker's Enlightenment Now: two Russian farmers, Boris and Igor. Boris has a goat and Igor doesn't. Igor complains to the authority that it isn't fair. Asked what he wants done, he says: kill Boris's goat. That ends the inequality, and now neither of them has a goat.
stories.insight: You can always achieve equality by making everyone poorer. Treating inequality means killing the goat; treating poverty means growth, which lets both men end up with more goats, even if unequally.
stories.quote: So the authority says, What do you want to do? And he says, Kill Boris's goat.

stories.topic: The CAA Protests and the Two Preambles
stories.summary: Asked about hope and despair, Amit points to one event that gave him both. He supported the anti-CAA protests and was heartened that young people across India took to the streets holding up the Preamble. What filled him with despair was that they held up Indira's Preamble, not Ambedkar's, and Indira's contains the word 'socialist'. He understands why: it also contains 'secular'. In Ambedkar's time the inclusion of both words was debated, and Ambedkar said no to both. On 'secular', his view was that if the value is inscribed in every article, stating it is mere signalling. On 'socialist', he held that the choice of economic system is a question for politics, not for the constitution. Ambedkar himself favoured a socialistic organisation at the time but changed his mind by the 1950s. Amit notes that Chandra Bhan Prasad told him his heroes are Ambedkar and Adam Smith.
stories.insight: A fashionable word can travel inside a cause you support. Ambedkar's own reasoning was that a constitution should leave economic choices to the democratic process rather than lock in an ideology, and his own changing views show why that matters.
stories.quote: what system of economic organization there should be is a question for politics, not for the constitution.

stories.topic: Sex Workers Talk Back on Live TV
stories.summary: Amit recalls a TV talk show hosted by Barkha Dutt where Kiran Bedi was being moralistic about prostitution. Actual sex workers on the show pushed back: they had entered the work willingly as the best option open to them, and they asked who she was to be so patronising and condescending about their choices. Amit wrote a column about it.
stories.insight: The people a moralistic ban claims to protect are often the ones resisting it. Criminalisation pushes the trade into the underworld, where trafficking and coercion actually flourish and victims can't safely go to the police.
stories.quote: there were actual sex workers there saying, Listen, we got into it willingly.

stories.summary: When homosexuality was effectively illegal under Section 377, cops ran an extortion scheme that Amit wrote about years ago in a column called 'The Matunga Racket'. They placed ads on online bulletin boards seeking gay men. Hapless respondents would go to the named railway station, often Matunga, where a plainclothes cop would meet them and threaten to tell their wife, father or family. The cops would then walk them to an ATM, use their card and empty the account. It was a common racket, and it became impossible once 377 was struck down.
stories.insight: Banning victimless acts between consenting adults does not end the behaviour. It hands the enforcers a weapon for extortion, and the people the law polices pay the price.
stories.quote: And they'd go with him to the ATM, they'd use his card, they'd empty it out.

stories.topic: The Child-Labour Bans Nobody Followed Up On
stories.summary: After Western activists complained about alleged sweatshops in Bangladesh, about 30,000 children were laid off. An Oxfam study found many of the girls went into prostitution and many of the boys turned to crime. In Nepal, after a scandal over children making carpets, 5,000 to 7,000 children were laid off, and a UNICEF study found the girls practically uniformly went into prostitution. Amit stresses that no parent wants their child in a factory; they do it because every other option is worse.
stories.insight: Feel-good bans can destroy the lives they claim to save. The campaigners declare victory and move on, and we only know the outcome because Oxfam and UNICEF happened to study it. The durable fix is rising family incomes, which means growth.
stories.quote: And no journalist who does these stories does a follow up on what happens to the children.

stories.summary: At a party a few days earlier, a successful professional from Hyderabad, sipping a single malt, told Amit that he found the word 'degrowth' very attractive and that India had had enough growth. Amit told him that he was free to say it, but that it was deeply immoral, because growth is what gets people out of poverty. By his account, over the last thirty years every one percent rise in India's GDP has lifted about two million people out of poverty.
stories.insight: Degrowth is a near-perfect luxury belief: costless and fashionable for the comfortable, ruinous for the poor. To someone who has already escaped poverty, two million is a statistic. To the people in it, it is better lives and better schools for their kids.
stories.quote: everything you're saying is deeply immoral because degrowth hurts the poor.

stories.topic: The Strongman Eventually Comes for the Rich
stories.summary: Ajay argues that business people who have economised on understanding the humanities and social sciences often make the error of allying with a strongman. The record is grim. In Saudi Arabia, MBS led a shakedown of hundreds of rich people and grabbed their wealth. In China, Xi Jinping attacked the rich, partly destroying and partly expropriating them. In Russia, Putin turned on the rich. In each case, individual billionaires believed they were insiders who would get special favours, and for a while it worked.
stories.insight: Populist leaders tend to be bad for growth and often turn on the businessmen who backed them. The only sustainable long-run recipe for building firms is rule of law and liberal democracy.
stories.quote: each individual billionaire at some point thought that No, no, no, I'm the insider I will get special favors by the government and for some time it seems to work. But in steady state it didn't.

recommendations.item: Nowhere Near
recommendations.creator: Yo La Tengo
recommendations.context: Mentioned in the opening chat, from the band Amit has been listening to a lot recently.
recommendations.reason: He calls it one of the great love songs.

recommendations.item: On Fire
recommendations.creator: Galaxie 500
recommendations.context: His 'first recommendation of the day', found through a Spotify shoegaze playlist. Galaxie 500 was Dean Wareham's band before Luna.
recommendations.reason: He calls it brilliant and says you've got to listen to it.

recommendations.item: Lunapark
recommendations.creator: Luna
recommendations.context: Luna was one of his favourite bands in the early-to-mid 90s, when he was deep into alternative rock in India.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a great album from an old love that the shoegaze rabbit hole brought back.

recommendations.item: November Rain
recommendations.creator: Guns N' Roses
recommendations.context: His instinctive answer to 'what's the most recent song you know?'
recommendations.reason: A song he knows and loves, and a marker of how long his musical clock had stood still.

recommendations.item: Sign of the Times
recommendations.creator: Harry Styles
recommendations.context: One of the only two post-1992 songs Ajay could name that he knows and loves.
recommendations.reason: He says Harry Styles is 'bloody good'.

recommendations.item: Shallow
recommendations.creator: Lady Gaga & Bradley Cooper
recommendations.context: The other recent song (2018) Ajay loves. Amit adds that there are some awesome covers of it.
recommendations.reason: A recent song that broke through Ajay's 90s-era taste.

recommendations.item: Troubled: A Memoir of Foster Care, Family, and Social Class
recommendations.creator: Rob Henderson
recommendations.context: Henderson's new book about growing up in foster homes, which Tyler Cowen also discussed on Marginal Revolution. Henderson coined 'luxury beliefs'.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls Henderson a very fine thinker worth following and highly recommends the book.

recommendations.item: Luxury Beliefs are Status Symbols
recommendations.creator: Rob Henderson
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes as the source of the concept the whole episode is built on.
recommendations.reason: Henderson's own account of how ideas that hurt the poor work as status markers for the elite.

recommendations.item: The Populist Playbook (Episode 42 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Referenced while explaining how words like populism, nationalism and socialism get misunderstood.
recommendations.reason: Covers how populism is confused with 'popular', plus tribalism and what happened to the Republican Party.

recommendations.item: The Citizenship Battles (Episode 152 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: His episode with Srinath Raghavan on the CAA, mentioned while describing the protests.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a great episode on the CAA and the protests against it.

recommendations.item: Caste, Capitalism and Chandra Bhan Prasad (Episode 296 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Brought up while discussing Ambedkar's later views on capitalism.
recommendations.reason: Prasad, a Dalit thinker, names Ambedkar and Adam Smith as his heroes, which helps show the full arc of Ambedkar's thinking.

recommendations.item: The Communist Manifesto
recommendations.creator: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels
recommendations.context: Ajay proposes an exercise during the socialism discussion.
recommendations.reason: Read the programme-for-action checklist at the end and you'll be astonished how much of it exists in modern India, which in many ways is the kind of paradise Marx and Engels wanted.

recommendations.item: Enlightenment Now
recommendations.creator: Steven Pinker
recommendations.context: The source of the Boris-and-Igor goat story.
recommendations.reason: Gives the sharpest illustration of why fixing inequality and fixing poverty are different things.

recommendations.item: Beware of These Five Fallacies! (Episode 45 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their previous episode, referenced for the zero-sum fallacy and the 'double thank you' moment.
recommendations.reason: Explains why we live in a positive-sum world, which is the foundation of the poverty-vs-inequality argument.

recommendations.item: India's Problem is Poverty, Not Inequality
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: His column, linked in the show notes alongside the inequality segment.
recommendations.reason: The full written version of his case that India must solve poverty through growth instead of chasing inequality.

recommendations.item: On Inequality
recommendations.creator: Harry Frankfurt
recommendations.context: Cited for its 'doctrine of sufficiency'.
recommendations.reason: A slim booklet giving a philosopher's version of the argument: what matters is that everyone has enough, not that everyone has the same. He says you should read it.

recommendations.item: Laws Against Victimless Crimes Should Be Scrapped
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: His 2008 piece, which he promises to link during the victimless-crimes segment.
recommendations.reason: Covers more angles on why banning consensual acts backfires.

recommendations.item: Poker and Life (Episode 38 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Referenced while arguing that betting should be legal.
recommendations.reason: Where they discussed that all of life is a gamble and that there is nothing inherently immoral about gambling.

recommendations.item: Bootleggers and Baptists: The Education of a Regulatory Economist
recommendations.creator: Bruce Yandle
recommendations.context: Cited in the discussion of alcohol prohibition.
recommendations.reason: Explains why moralists who demand a ban and the underworld that profits from it end up on the same side.

recommendations.item: Raees: An Empty Shell of a Gangster Film
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: His review of the Shah Rukh Khan film, which casts a bootlegger as the enemy of a prohibitionist politician.
recommendations.reason: Shows how the film gets the real-world politics backwards, as Yandle's essay would predict.

recommendations.item: The Matunga Racket
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: His 2007 column on cops extorting gay men while Section 377 was in force.
recommendations.reason: A concrete case of the harm done by criminalising a victimless act.

recommendations.item: Why Children Labour
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: His 2007 column on child labour, which links to the relevant studies.
recommendations.reason: Lays out what actually happened to children laid off after Western campaigns, and why growth is the long-term fix.

recommendations.item: The Economics of Child Labor
recommendations.creator: Kaushik Basu and Pham Hoang Van
recommendations.context: One of the studies he names during the child-labour discussion.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a great study of the family-income threshold that determines whether children work or go to school.

recommendations.item: Observations on International Labor Standards and Trade
recommendations.creator: Alan B Krueger
recommendations.context: Named alongside Basu's work in the child-labour discussion.
recommendations.reason: Another 'great study' supporting the case that prosperity, not blunt bans, ends child labour.

recommendations.item: Child Labor in the Global Economy
recommendations.creator: Eric V Edmonds and Nina Pavcnik
recommendations.context: The third body of research he cites on child labour.
recommendations.reason: Adds to the evidence that rising incomes are what keep children out of work.

recommendations.item: Price Controls Lead to Shortages and Harm the Poor
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked from the price-controls segment, where he promises to link his pieces on the subject.
recommendations.reason: His fuller case that price caps destroy the price signal and create shortages that hit the poor hardest.

recommendations.item: The Vision of the Anointed: Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy
recommendations.creator: Thomas Sowell
recommendations.context: He reads a long passage from it while explaining why people hold luxury beliefs.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a great book that gets to the heart of the problem: it shows that the moral vanity behind luxury beliefs is at least 200 years old.

recommendations.item: Defending the Undefendable
recommendations.creator: Walter Block
recommendations.context: His closing reading recommendation. He hints they may one day do an episode with that title.
recommendations.reason: Block, an Austrian economist, defends ideas usually considered beyond the pale, much as Amit defended sweatshops and legal prostitution in this episode. He calls it beautiful and important: you needn't agree, but it trains you to think differently instead of swallowing a tribe's dogma.

core_ideas.explanation: Rob Henderson's term for fashionable ideas that make elites feel virtuous and give them status, at almost no cost to themselves, while the costs land on the poor. Amit's test comes from Gandhi: judge every policy first by its impact on the poor. In a poor country like India, where ending poverty is a moral imperative, the beliefs that fail this test include socialism, inequality-obsession, banning victimless crimes, anti-capitalism and price controls.
core_ideas.quote: Luxury beliefs are ideas and opinions that confer status on the upper class while often inflicting costs on the lower classes.

core_ideas.concept: Socialism Means Coercion, Not 'Good for Society'
core_ideas.explanation: People hear 'socialism' as caring for society, but strictly it means the state owning much of the property and regulating the rest. Freedom then becomes something the state grants you, and you become a subject rather than a citizen. Amit frames politics around consent versus coercion and reads the 20th century as the failure of socialism. India's socialist decades kept hundreds of millions poor for longer than necessary. Ajay adds that much of the Communist Manifesto's programme for action is visible in modern India.
core_ideas.quote: for me, the two words that I really care about and think about are consent and coercion. Right? I care deeply about consent. It has an absolute value. And socialism is equal to coercion.

core_ideas.concept: Poverty, Not Inequality, Is the Problem
core_ideas.explanation: In a zero-sum world poverty and inequality would move together, but the world is positive-sum. Growth lifts the poor while lifting the rich more, so inequality can rise while poverty falls, which is what happened in India after 1991. Treating inequality means redistribution, which kills Boris's goat. Treating poverty means growth. Redistribution is cognitively easier to sell and makes its advocates feel virtuous, which is why the inequality frame keeps winning even though it drives the country backwards.
core_ideas.quote: In which of these two countries would you rather be poor, the USA or Bangladesh? And the answer everybody will say I would rather be poor in the USA. But the truth is that the USA has greater inequality, Bangladesh has greater poverty. Poverty is the key.

core_ideas.explanation: Harry Frankfurt's alternative to egalitarianism. Instead of equalising, define what is enough for a person to live on and get everyone to that level. It works as a proxy for eliminating poverty, a test on which, Amit says, every Indian government has failed.
core_ideas.quote: the doctrine of sufficiency is that you define what is enough for a man to live on. Right, you define that. And then you try to get everyone to that level. That is what matters.

core_ideas.concept: 200 Basis Points and the Power of Compounding
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's reply to wise seniors who say a little inequality-chasing won't hurt growth much. Take a growth-hostile, redistributionist policy environment at about 2% per-capita growth and a modest pro-growth one at 4%, with no South Korea-style leaps. By the rule of 70, 2% doubles incomes in 35 years and quadruples them in 70. Ajay puts 4% at roughly 16 years to double and 32 to quadruple. Thirty-two years is within a young person's planning horizon; seventy is barely imaginable. A gap that sounds small becomes a generation of lost prosperity.
core_ideas.quote: You think only 200 basis points, but there's a power of compounding.

core_ideas.concept: Banning Victimless Crimes Hands Them to the Underworld
core_ideas.explanation: A right-wing luxury belief: ban prostitution, betting and alcohol because they are immoral. The activity continues, but in the underworld, where cops are paid off, the rule of law doesn't reach, and trafficking, match-fixing and spurious liquor flourish. Victims can't go to the police. In the Netherlands, regulated brothels advertise openly and sex workers have rights, pay taxes and face little crime. England has legal betting and taxes the houses rather than the gamblers. Legal activity can be regulated, its balance sheets inspected and its abusers prosecuted. Amit's line is that the left should accept freedom in the marketplace and the right should accept freedom in the bedroom.
core_ideas.quote: Your main principle should be consenting adults should be free to do whatever they want with each other, as long as they're not harming anyone else.

core_ideas.explanation: Bruce Yandle's insight: the moralist who campaigns for a ban and the bootlegger who profits from it want the same thing. That is why Amit faults the film Raees, where Shah Rukh Khan's bootlegger treats a prohibitionist politician as an enemy. In reality, the bootlegger would be funding him.
core_ideas.quote: In the real world, the Shah Rukh character bootlegger is funding the politician. Because as long as alcohol stays illegal, he has business.

core_ideas.explanation: Anti-capitalists conflate free markets with cronyism. Businesses always try to ally with the state and use its power to keep competitors out, and that is crony capitalism. True free markets need the state only for rule of law, and in them the only way to get rich is to serve people, the 'double thank you' exchange. Companies like Amazon grew by making millions of lives better, which is why even its critics order from it.
core_ideas.quote: pro-business and pro market can mean opposite things.

core_ideas.explanation: People work in sweatshops because it is the best option open to them. Banning the sweatshop removes that option and leaves worse ones, as the Bangladesh and Nepal child-labour layoffs showed. Child labour is horrible, but the way to end it is to raise family incomes above the threshold at which parents send children to school instead of work, which requires growth rather than blunt 'ban it, campaign against it' tools.
core_ideas.quote: Those people chose to work in a sweatshop because it was the best option open to them. Respect their agency, respect their decision.

core_ideas.explanation: Prices signal the world's scarcities and constraints and give people an incentive to produce more. Cap them and you get shortages and black markets. In Amit's thought experiment, capping cars at ten thousand rupees would kill the industry and push the few remaining cars onto the black market. In reality, a price cap on stents led to stent shortages and people died. Banning Uber surge pricing means first-come-first-served, so the person rushing to a hospital or a flight loses out. Amit ties this to the Yes Minister logic: we must do something, this is something, let's do it.
core_ideas.quote: If you take that information away, you are always going to have scarcities.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay, as an economist, looks for the optimisation behind the beliefs. The cynical answer is 'I've got mine, so it costs me nothing', though that doesn't explain why these particular beliefs. His hypotheses: (1) philanthropy-style insurance, where pious positions buy safety from future pitchforks and from a populist state; (2) fashion, where moral fervour is valued over intellectual capability and makes you look caring and likeable; (3) cheap signalling, where unlike a Louis Vuitton bag, talk is a free badge of club membership and status; (4) Timur Kuran's preference falsification, where people say whatever helps them gain influence or safety. The equilibrium needs intellectual soft-headedness: a broad base of doctor-engineer capabilities with little social science or humanities, so few people call out the claims. Some adopt these views out of self-interest and become a kernel that others gather around, until the beliefs become a pattern.
core_ideas.quote: To buy a Louis Vuitton is at least expensive. Here it's talk. Talk is free.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit credits most believers with good intentions. We signal virtue to ourselves as much as to others, and holding the right opinion feels like doing good. Social media sharpens this. To belong, you join a tribe and accept its dogmas, then attack the other side, then attack your own side for impurity, which is why so much cancellation comes from within. Having publicly committed, ego makes you double down. Amit says his own silly Marx-and-Engels opinions at 17 or 18 might have hardened that way if they had lived on in screenshots.
core_ideas.quote: we lie to ourselves as much as we lie to others.

core_ideas.explanation: Thomas Sowell's diagnosis in The Vision of the Anointed. The prevailing vision offers believers a special state of grace: they are not just correct but morally superior, and dissenters are not just wrong but sinful, to be enlightened or exposed. Sowell argues this structure hasn't changed in at least 200 years. Amit uses it to show that luxury beliefs are an old human tendency that social media amplifies, not a new invention.
core_ideas.quote: Those who accept this vision are deemed to be not merely factually correct, but morally on a higher plane. Put differently, those who disagree with the prevailing vision are seen as being not merely in error, but in sin.

core_ideas.concept: Firm on Values, Open on Facts
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's closing counsel. Don't accept a tribe's dogma from A to Z. If you never disagree with your side on anything, something is wrong. You don't need an opinion on everything, especially one formed in 30 seconds for a tweet. Hold your values firmly, but treat the facts of a complex world with humility and listen to those who disagree.
core_ideas.quote: when it comes to values, be firm on your values. When it comes to the facts of the world, the world is deeply complex. Be open, listen to people who disagree with you. That's the only way to grow.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Asked why they are colour-coordinated in shades of blue, Amit replies: 'maybe we both love the blues.'

While Amit waxes lyrical about shoegaze, Ajay muses that inferring genre from a track is 'a nice Bayes theorem application.' Amit protests: 'I'm talking about art, I'm talking about music, I'm talking about the soul.'
After Ajay names 'Shallow', Amit proposes a duet: 'You and I should perform Shallow sometimes. I'll do the high parts.'
Ajay says 32 years is a practical horizon for their young editor Nomsita. Amit: 'thirty-two years later she'll be younger than you are now.'
Amit addresses 'dear listener'. Ajay corrects him, keeping up the show's 'gentle reader' running gag: 'We are not listeners, we are readers.'
Amit rejects euphemism: 'You and I are prostitutes, we're selling our services for money... I do a lot of things free even. So I'm even worse.'
Having bashed the left, Amit turns even-handed: 'we've been shitting on the left, as indeed we should, but we should also shit on the right.'
In the price-control thought experiment, Amit tells viewers to pause the video and think, asks 'Have you paused?', and freezes like a statue himself.

Amit, after a long tirade: 'I have ranted and raved, which is my elite privilege. It is a luxury that I get to enjoy.' Ajay begins his reply: 'because I'm a card carrying economist, okay, and here is my card.'
Amit's aphorism: 'those who signal the most virtue possess the least... I have found this to be true especially of men, so watch out.'
Amit's caricature of the luxury-belief holder: elites in air-conditioned living rooms, typing on MacBooks, discussing 'which luxury headphone to buy next to add to the three they already have.'
Amit on instant Twitter experts: 'You've thought about that for thirty seconds. I have read about it for thirty years.'
Rob Henderson, who coined 'luxury beliefs', and Tyler Cowen's blog Marginal Revolution, which discussed Henderson's memoir.
Gandhi's dictum that the first thing to consider about any policy is its impact on the poor, which Amit uses as his yardstick throughout.
'Hamara socialism achha tha': Amit's impression of older, elite guests on The Seen and the Unseen who are nostalgic for the socialist era. One even lamented the fall of the Soviet Union.
Yes Minister: 'we must do something, this is something, let's do it.' Amit uses it to describe lazy, feel-good policymaking such as price controls.
Hansie Cronje: Amit argues that cricketers now earn so much that the incentive to fix matches is lower than 'in the Hansie Cronje days.'
Amit wants to see HDFC, Axis Bank and HSBC open betting outlets, so you could bet from an account the way you trade from a demat account.
Section 377, the law under which homosexuality was effectively illegal in India until it was struck down, which made the Matunga extortion racket possible.
Timur Kuran's 'preference falsification', which Ajay invokes to explain why people publicly profess beliefs that help them get ahead.
Amit to the degrowth enthusiast, in Hindi: you can say whatever fashionable thing you want sitting in Sweden, but growth is what gets Indians out of poverty.
Amit says social media plays to 'the worst demons of our nature, as it were, instead of the better angels', a twist on the phrase 'the better angels of our nature'.
